      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>“On the 21st he received intelligence of the enemy</Line>
        <Line>having advancing by Coma, with 12,000 infantry, and</Line>
        <Line>4000 horse. He gave orders for the army to fall back the</Line>
        <Line>same night to a position extending from Tarragona to Tu-</Line>
        <Line>dela, the last point to be occupied by the army of Arra-</Line>
        <Line>gon, and the fifth division of the centre, which was in</Line>
        <Line>Caparossa. Notwithstanding this movement, the army</Line>
        <Line>continued to retreat, in the darkness of the night, with</Line>
        <Line>considerable trouble, and the division reached their re-</Line>
        <Line>spective points, by marching that night and the following</Line>
        <Line>day, for some detention arose from the removal of the ar-</Line>
        <Line>tillery from Cintruenigo, and on the 22d the four divisions</Line>
        <Line>of the army were in the position which they had to occupy,</Line>
        <Line>without having sustained any loss. On the 23d the ad-</Line>
        <Line>vanced parties reported that three columns of the enemy</Line>
        <Line>were marching in the direction of Tudela; the generale</Line>
        <Line>was beaten, and while troops of dragoons were passing</Line>
        <Line>the bridge, the enemy occupied the points of attack,</Line>
        <Line>which began at eight o’clock in the morning: at ten o’clock</Line>
        <Line>the whole line was engaged. Our troops maintained their</Line>
        <Line>position with the utmost valour, and the enemy was re-</Line>
        <Line>pulsed on all sides. He renewed the attack, and rendered</Line>
        <Line>himself master of an olive grove on the left, whence he de-</Line>
        <Line>scended with a tremendous fire, but was so well received</Line>
        <Line>by our gallant troops; that after a most obstinate conflict</Line>
        <Line>he was compelled to retreat. While our troops were pur-</Line>
        <Line>suing the defeated enemy on our left, another division of</Line>
        <Line>the enemy penetrated through Tudela on the right, and</Line>
        <Line>took our pursuing troops in the rear: this decided the fate</Line>
        <Line>of the day, and nothing was left for our army but to re-</Line>
        <Line>treat to Borja. While this was going forward in Tudela,</Line>
        <Line>the fourth division, commanded by Gen. Lapena, which</Line>
        <Line>was in Cascante, two hours march from the field of battle,</Line>
        <Line>which had received orders to attack the right flank of the</Line>
        <Line>enemy, found 3000 French infantry and 1000 cavalry op-</Line>
        <Line>posed to them, in the act of offering battle; Lapena im-</Line>
        <Line>mediately engaged, defeated, and pursued them to the</Line>
        <Line>heights of Tudela, whence he was attacked by the enemy’s</Line>
        <Line>troops, who occupied the heights. Lapena retreated to</Line>
        <Line>the position of Cascante, where he defeated the enemy,</Line>
        <Line>and at the fall of night, began to fall back to Borja, ac-</Line>
        <Line>cording to the last order he received. On his retreat he</Line>
        <Line>was again attacked by the enemy, but our troops checked</Line>
        <Line>his progress, and the four divisions reached Borja, whence</Line>
        <Line>they marched to Catalayud. The forces of the enemy in</Line>
        <Line>these actions of Tudela and Cascante, amounted to from</Line>
        <Line>36 to 40,000, and from 6 to 7000 cavalry. Their loss</Line>
        <Line>has been very considerable, as has been ours in missing and</Line>
        <Line>prisoners.”</Line>

        <Line>In a letter of the 27th, Gen. Castanos sends advice, that</Line>

        <Line>having received notice, that the enemy threatened to at-</Line>
        <Line>tack Samosierra, for these reasons, and wishing to be near</Line>
        <Line>the capital in case the French should endeavour to advance</Line>
        <Line>to it, he had determined to go to Seguenza. The Major</Line>
        <Line>General, Don Benito St. Juan, posted in the Puerto (post</Line>
        <Line>of Samosierra), sends advice in a letter of the 28th of this</Line>
        <Line>month, that at break of day that morning the division of</Line>
        <Line>troops under his command were alarmed, and immediately</Line>
        <Line>under arms, expecting to be attacked in force by the ene-</Line>
        <Line>my, as all the advices received during the night concurred</Line>
        <Line>in stating, that on the morning on the preceding day great</Line>
        <Line>numbers of the enemy’s troops had defiled by Aranda de</Line>
        <Line>Duero, directing their march to the encampments of Bo-</Line>
        <Line>ciguillas and La Grange, with many pieces of artillery</Line>
        <Line>and other ordinary stores. Accordingly, a little after six</Line>
        <Line>in the morning, were heard in the heights of Samosierra,</Line>
        <Line>various discharges of artillery and small arms continually</Line>
        <Line>increasing, and were in the direction of the pass of Sepul-</Line>
        <Line>veda, which left no doubt that an attack would be made,</Line>
        <Line>and though he could confide in the resistance of the brave</Line>
        <Line>garrison, which had been reinforced the day before (the</Line>
        <Line>27th), with 1000 fusileers of the regiment of Jaen, the num-</Line>
        <Line>bers of the enemy could not but excite solicitude, and from</Line>
        <Line>the moment of the attack proper measures were taken to send</Line>
        <Line>succours of infantry, artillery, and ammunition; but with-</Line>
        <Line>out the assistance of these he effected the complete defence</Line>
        <Line>of this point, notwithstanding the attack lasted more than</Line>
        <Line>four hours; the enemy having attacked with 4000 infantry,</Line>
        <Line>1600 cavalry, and four pieces of cannon, besides the re-</Line>
        <Line>inforcements which were at hand to support their troops.</Line>
      </Paragraph>

        <Line>day, by the enemy, with from 1500 to 4000 infantry,</Line>
        <Line>1500 cavalry, and four pieces of artillery, and that he</Line>
        <Line>had repulsed them with glory to the arms of the king and</Line>
        <Line>country. He proposes soon to send the circumstantial de-</Line>
        <Line>tails of the action, in which he says, we have suffered</Line>
        <Line>some loss, but he supposes that of the enemy must have</Line>
        <Line>been double, the firing having continued till ten o’clock.</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>According to the last</Line>

        <Line>peror with the highest distinction, and accompanies</Line>
        <Line>him in all his hunting parties. All the efforts of the</Line>
        <Line>English to recover their influence over this Sovereign</Line>
        <Line>have failed.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>FROM THE AMERICAN PAPERS.</Line>

      <DateLine>
        <Line>WASHINGTON, Nov. 8.—</Line>
      </DateLine>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>This day the following</Line>
        <Line>Message, with the several documents accompanying</Line>
        <Line>it, was presented to both Houses:—</Line>

        <Line>MESSAGE TO THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF REPRESENTA-</Line>
        <Line>TIVES OF THE UNITED STATES.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>“It would have been a source, fellow-citizens, of</Line>
        <Line>much gratification, if our last communications from Europe</Line>
        <Line>had enabled me to inform you, that the Belligerent Na-</Line>
        <Line>tions, whose disregard of neutral right has been so de-</Line>
        <Line>structive to our commerce, had become awakened to the</Line>
        <Line>duty and the policy of revoking their unrighteous edicts.</Line>
        <Line>That no means might be omitted to produce this salutary</Line>
        <Line>effect, I lost no time in availing myself of the Act autho-</Line>
        <Line>rising a suspension, in whole, or in part, of the several</Line>
        <Line>Embargo Laws. Our Ministers at London and Paris</Line>
        <Line>were instructed to explain to the respective Governments</Line>
        <Line>there, our disposition to exercise the authority in such</Line>
        <Line>manner as would withdraw the pretext on which the ag-</Line>
        <Line>gressions were originally founded, and open the way for</Line>
        <Line>a renewal of that commercial intercourse, which it was</Line>
        <Line>alleged on all sides had been reluctantly obstructed. As</Line>
        <Line>each of these Governments had pledged its readiness to</Line>
        <Line>concur in renouncing a measure, which reached its adver-</Line>
        <Line>sary through the incontestible rights of neutrals only, and</Line>

Here in a space no larger than the state of Texas, Nature has painted one of her incomparable canvases. Virgin forests alternate with fertile fields; high wooded slopes separate verdant valleys; famous old cities are reflected in historic rivers; and to the traveller who, maybe, is revisiting the scene after an absence of many years there rises on the joyous wave of recollection the memory of impressive cathedrals, priceless art treasures and the inspir- ing messages of a Bach, a Beethoven or a Richard Wagner. Despite the utilitarian trend of the age, Germany is still replete with romance and poetry; every city is an eloquent chronicler of the old as well as of the new, and it is the old, the picturesque, the unique of which people come in quest when penetrating to the heart of a foreign country. BREMEN, so the uninitiated might be inclined to think, is like every other port merely a point of ingress and egress. But this feeling is dispelled from the moment the incoming traveller finds himself standing in the chief square surrounded by the most im- pressive monuments of medieval archi- tecture to be found in all Germany. Here is the Town Hall with its famous winding staircase dating from the golden period of the German Renais- sance; the Merchant's Exchange with its fine old Guild Hall; the eight hundred year old Cathedral; and as an impressive reminder of Bremen's early history, the awe-inspiring Roland Statue, betokening the municipal free- dom granted to this member of the trinity of old Hanseatic cities. If you have travelled by a North-German- Lloyd boat you will be interested in the magnificent building housing this far- flung shipping line. COLOGNE. A story is told of an Amer- ican traveller who went to Cologne, drank in the beauty of the incompa- rable Cathedral, studied its gracious ar- ches, its stone traceries, its heaven- piercing towers from every angle, and then turned about and went back home, saying that he did not wish to have this impression effaced by further sight- seeing. This, however, was to do scant justice to the other beauties of the old city. There are the churches saturated in legendary lore, the interesting street life, the graceful bridges thrown across the Rhine, and the ever-shifting pic- ture of the river traffic. From one of the far-flung towers of the Cathedral an incomparable panorama of the Rhine with its castles and vineyards unrolls itself on a clear day. DUSSELDORF is the hub of Ger- many's industrial wheel, but unlike the great steel and iron center of Penn- sylvania, it is as beautifully spotless with its flowerdecked parks and garden lawns as any city in that wonderland of California. Düsseldorf disproves the theory that a man may not serve two masters, as here is not only to be found the center of Rhenish art, but also the center of Rhenish industry and trade. The Düsseldorf school of painting still maintains its supremacy. Again new and old are here thrown together in happy confusion, and many visitors will be ready to agree with the native population who pronounce Düs- seldorf the most beautiful modern city in Germany. HAMBURG is so essentially an Eng- lish speaking city that some wag has suggested the posting of notices an- nouncing: "German also spoken here!" To be seen at its best Hamburg needs the glorifying sunshine when the waters of the big inland basin sparkle like silver, and the homes of the Ham- burg patrician families gleam out of the surrounding foliage like veritable fairy palaces. Hamburg has not only its magnificent modern harbor where ships from every port sail in and out, but there is also a fascinating "old Hamburg," where quaint houses bend forward to gossip across the narrow streets, and where one may see the humble dwelling in which Johannes Brahms, Hamburg's great son, first saw the light of day. Or if you prefer zoology to music, you may turn your steps to the vast park where Hagen- beck's collection of wild animals roam about at will as if in their native haunts. HEIDELBERG, renowned in song and story! No one can escape the spell of the city so "rich in honors" apostrophized by the German poet Heine, in his famous lines. Heidelberg Castle is like some powerful monarch of the Middle Ages whom centuries have not succeeded in deposing from his throne. But while the Castle with its marvellous natural beauty and historic associations remains the crowning glory of the place, the old city down in the valley is rapidly fol- lowing the trend of modern life and with its excellent hotels and its in- teresting summer program of Music Festivals, exhibitions and aquatic sports makes a manifold appeal to those who like historic gems in modern settings. MUNICH is a lovable city, a quality to be ascribed to the proverbial "Ge- mütlichkeit" of the Bavarian charac- ter. Give the people their art, their music, their Carnival privileges (just restored) and their beer, and they ask nothing more of life. This "joy of living" proves infectious and strang- ers linger gladly within the walls. All Munich is a vast Museum with in- teresting architectural monuments and picturesque corners at every turn. The Wagnerian performances at the Prince Regent Theatre are unsurpas- sable and these alone would make Munich the Mecca of music lovers. The wonderful panorama of the Ba- varian Highlands stretches up to the very gates of Munich, and luxurious motor buses carry tourists to the twin cities of Garmisch-Partenkirchen; to Oberammergau, the home of the Pas- sion Play; and to the romantic castles built by Wagner's friend, the "mad king of Bavaria." NUREMBERG owes its perennial popularity to its Old World atmos- phere, to the impressive picturesque- ness of its medieval architecture, and to the enduring monuments of iron and stone, of song and story, of the brush and the pen left by such mas- ters as Albrecht Dürer, Hans Sachs, Melanchton, Peter Vischer, Veit Stoss, Adam Krafft, and an illustrious line of craftsmen who lived at a time in the world's history when men "worked for the joy of the working!" In the Germanic Museum, the history of German civilization may be traced as clearly as if one were turning the pages of a volume of old prints. The visitor wanders about enchanted among the churches, richly-wrought fountains, and palaces of the erstwhile Nuremberg patricians, and then up the hill to the old fortress crowning the summit, there to look out over the "sea of roofs" and drink in the beauty of the mise-en-scene. WIESBADEN is an old Roman bath, these early invaders of Northern Europe having discovered the efficacy of its hot springs. A spring "cure" in Wiesbaden belongs to the regular rou- tine of every aristocratic German, and foreigners were not slow to discover the intimate charm of the place and the stimulating society. Wiesbaden specializes, as it were, in music, and the periodic Festivals bring together the best that Germany has to offer in the way of creative and interpretat- ive artists. Situated as it is in the heart of the Taunus, Wiesbaden is singularly blessed with interesting ob- jectives, both for pedestrians and motorists and every day a new pro- spect opens up for those who wish some more active sort of life than strolling through the beautiful walks or assembling for bridge and gossip at the Casino. Stuttgart Offers Visitors Many Historical Features (Tribune Press Service). STUTTGART, May 5.—Owing to the charm and attraction of its historical buildings and associations, Stuttgart, the capital of Wurtemburg, offers to visitors a great variety of interesting features. The river Neckar flows through the town, which is beautifully situated in a valley surrounded by fo- rested hills. The first authentic evidence of Stuttgart's existence dates from 1229. It originally consisted of the old town, walled-in by ramparts, which were demolished in 1660, and suburbs. The old town has picturesque, narrow, winding streets; the new town, on the contrary, is characterized by broad thoroughfares, part of which have been constructed in terrace-like shape on the slopes of the surrounding hills, and by modern buildings. Stuttgart is frequently called the most beautiful of Germany's large towns, and is rich in places of interest. The town has a very mild climate and is very healthy. It is a climatic resort in the spring and fall, and has a well patronized spa with mineral baths. The sanitary conditions of the town are perfect. Innumerable visitors from all parts of the world frequent, and make Stuttgart their centre. The po- pulation is about three hundred and fifty thousand and the town has an important industry of cotton goods, paperware, leatherware, musical and optical instruments, motors, motor- cars, machines etc. There is also a large bookselling trade and many print- ing works. In the State Library, there is a large collection of bibles in over one hun- dred languages, and many valuable old manuscripts. Schiller was educated at the Academy and wrote his "Räu- ber" there. The place is noted for its fine collections of antiquities, en- gravings etc., and for its private art collections. The theatres, concerts and other entertainments are of a high- class order. Thanks to many mineral springs of various description, Wurtemburg has earned wide celebrity, and a number of universally renowned resorts have come into existence. The climatic conditions are particularly favorable for agriculture, fruit and wine growing, etc.; art and science are fostered with especial care; and there are many ex- cellently preserved antiquities, famous art museums, interesting buildings and beautiful landscapes, all of which con- cur to render Wurtemburg singu- larly attractive to travellers from abroad. The reputation of Stuttgart for its well-managed hotels has long been very high. Amongst those hotels, which can be very warmly recommend- ed are the Marquart, Continental and Victoria. BAD EMS IS SPA AND ALSO MERRY HOLIDAY CENTER (Tribune Press Service). BAD EMS, May 5.—The famous "Ems telegram" has found its way into history. It was in Ems that the French Ambassador had his last in- terview with the old Kaiser before the war of 1870. In fact, Ems is a place of many memories. The old German Emperor came here for many years and this lovely resort has been patron- ized by such visitors as the Russian Emperor, King Leopold of Belgium, the kings of Sweden, Saxony and Bavaria. They were all attracted to this place by the cure of throat and digestive ail- ments for which Ems is so justly famed. Ems has a long Anglo-Saxon tradition, and the numerous visitors, invalids and holiday makers, and the leading opera singers of Europe and America are in the habit of coming here at the end of the season, in order to enjoy the special treatment which it provides for their special troubles or relaxation. Ems waters, Ems pastilles and Ems salts are known everywhere. They are all supplied by the State Domain in a purely natural condition. The resort is famed for its eminently suc- cessful cures and for the following complaints: catarrh of the respira- tory, digestive and abdominal organs; diseases of women; asthma; emphy- sema; influenza and its resulting af- fections; diseases of the heart and disorder of the blood circulation; arte- riosclerosis; gout and rheumatism. The State Institute of Medical Re- search is fitted up with all the latest requirements of contemporary science. There are natural carbonic acid baths, inhalatoria and pneumatic chambers. All the methods of treatment at Ems are thoroughly up-to-date. Amongst the attractions to be found at Ems are: Excellent concerts, fine operatic and dramatic performances, festival plays with characteristic local features, regattas, children's entertain- ments, illuminations, lawn-tennis, hoc- key, swimming, rowing, sailing, shoot- ing, fishing etc. There are lovely walks in the surrounding forests and motor tours in the valleys of the Rhine, Mo- selle and Lahn, in the Taunus hills, the Westerwald, the Hunsruck and the Eifel. It would be difficult for any visitor to Ems not to feel that at last he had discovered a holiday centre after his own heart. The keynotes of the place are tranquillity and refinement. Munich Is Lure For Art Students And Tourists MUNICH, May 5.—Munich, with its enormous libraries, its fine museums, its splendid brewing facilities and its many German Renaissance buildings, remains the Bavarian centre for tour- ists, as well as art students, from all countries of the world. Principal among the attractions of the city are the art museums, richly stored with treasures representing all ages and countries. The Old and New Pinakothek and the Glyptothek stand high among Continental museums, with their splendid collections of paintings and sculpture, while several other buildings devoted to scientific and ethnological displays make the city important to the world of science, as well as to that of art. Many of the city's fifteenth century buildings are still standing and are remarkably preserved, and the modern districts are, for the most part, built in a style which blends harmoniously with the architectural relies of earlier ages. Hotel accommodations in Munich, as a result of the heavy tourist traffic each year are plentiful and are among the finest provided in Bavaria. Many interesting excursions into the sur- rounding countryside and the Bavar- ian Alps are provided at moderate prices for visitors to the ancient ca- pital. RESORT ARRIVALS (Tribune Press Service). GOOD HOTEL ACCOMMODATION ALL KINDS OF SPORTS American Support Given To Gutenberg Society MAYENCE, May 5.—Mr. Bartlett, the New York Publisher, who is stay- ing at Mayence at present, has pre- sented the sum of one thousand dol- lars to the Gutenberg Society of this town, the birthplace of Gutenberg, for the purpose of assisting the society to realize some of the aims it has set be- fore itself in connection with the Gutenberg Museum. This contribution is supplementary to the five thousand dollars already presented by this same well-wisher, on the occasion of the Gutenberg Jubilee, in 1925. Mayence, the old Roman Moguntia- cum, was well known to chroniclers in the Middle Ages as "the golden pin- nacle of the German Empire" and ce- lebrated by them as the home of Frauenlob and Gutenberg. Considered from the standpoints of history and art, Mayence is undoubtedly one of the most important towns on the Rhine. Situated as it is amidst lovely sur- roundings, it is also one of the most picturesque sites on a river justly famed for wonderful scenery—the Rhine. The Electors of Mayence formerly resided here, and the town is full of reminiscences of a great historic past, containing as it does many noteworthy edifices, both sacred and profane. The Town is characterized by a num- ber of wonderfully picturesque old streets and lanes and squares, by the interesting mansions of the patricians, and palaces of the nobility with their ancient courtyards and gateways. There are some world-famous collec- tions in the numerous Galleries, Mu- seums, Libraries etc. All parts of the Rhine and its adjacent valleys are easily accessible by rail or steamer.       <Heading type="main">
        <Line>THE FARMER'S CORN.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line><Initial type="simple">A</Initial>t early dawn, when o’er the leaves</Line>
        <Line>The hoar-frost creeps and steals their</Line>
        <Line>bloom,</Line>
        <Line>When trees stand stiff in gloom</Line>
        <Line>Beneath the sunless morn,</Line>
        <Line>Old Farmer John salutes his sheaves</Line>
        <Line>Of ripened corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Bright jewels 'mong the stubble gleam,</Line>
        <Line>And sparkle from his careless tread,</Line>
        <Line>And gossamer, outspread,</Line>
        <Line>Enrobes the naked thorn;</Line>
        <Line>But Farmer John, to all a dream,</Line>
        <Line>Moves through his corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The startled hare before him springs,</Line>
        <Line>And down the furrow speeds like wind,</Line>
        <Line>While crisp leaves spirt behind;</Line>
        <Line>The yellow mists, upborne,</Line>
        <Line>Skim o'er the vale on noiseless wings</Line>
        <Line>Above the corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>But Farmer John with anxious eyes</Line>
        <Line>The struggling streaks of dawn surveys,</Line>
        <Line>And through the spreading haze</Line>
        <Line>That veils the face of morn</Line>
        <Line>A blood-red rim he sees arise</Line>
        <Line>To greet his corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>And fear creeps through his trembling veins</Line>
        <Line>As the rising sun dilates in red,</Line>
        <Line>And as each mountain's head</Line>
        <Line>His crimson hues adorn,</Line>
        <Line>John quakes to think the coming rains</Line>
        <Line>May swamp his corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Still high o'erhead the waning moon</Line>
        <Line>Reveals a patch of clearing blue,</Line>
        <Line>And hope comes peering through</Line>
        <Line>With Luna's welcome horn,</Line>
        <Line>That yet a favoring sky at noon</Line>
        <Line>Will bless the corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The changeful sun, erst steeped in fire,</Line>
        <Line>Behold, pours fourth rich amber streams</Line>
        <Line>That quench with bright joy-gleams</Line>
        <Line>The frowns his face had worn,</Line>
        <Line>For Heaven and he may now conspire</Line>
        <Line>To save the corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>See, o'er the east a golden mantle's flung!</Line>
        <Line>Fast move the mists from out the north,</Line>
        <Line>And as the winds come forth,</Line>
        <Line>To little shreds are torn</Line>
        <Line>The great cloud-masses that o'erhung</Line>
        <Line>The golden corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>And lo! the wakened crows soar high;</Line>
        <Line>How arrow-straight they upward fly</Line>
        <Line>O'er bits of dappled sky,</Line>
        <Line>And leave the earth forlorn!</Line>
        <Line>While clouds of lazy rooks float by</Line>
        <Line>The tempting corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>What smiles sleep in the farmer's eyes!</Line>
        <Line>To-day he'll "in" that precious grain,</Line>
        <Line>For he knows the dreaded rain</Line>
        <Line>Such bodings dare not scorn.</Line>
        <Line>So, whistling thanks to sun and skies.</Line>
        <Line>He leaves the corn.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>ONE OF THE SMITH FAMILY.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line><Initial type="simple">M</Initial>r. Fitzwalter was the pastor of an</Line>
        <Line>impoverished but genteel colored con-</Line>
        <Line>gregation in Port Royal, and for Mr.</Line>
        <Line>Fitzwalter I had a rooted if an ungodly</Line>
        <Line>aversion, founded upon the two trifling</Line>
        <Line>facts that he grinned at the beginning</Line>
        <Line>and the close of every remark he ut-</Line>
        <Line>tered, and that in conversing he always</Line>
        <Line>picked out the showiest words in the dic-</Line>
        <Line>tionary, with more regard to sound than</Line>
        <Line>sense. However, he had a poor sick</Line>
        <Line>wife, and in consequence I frequently</Line>
        <Line>visited the Fitzwalter's apartment, and</Line>
        <Line>always found the family poor indeed.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"You have no relations here," I said</Line>
        <Line>to Mrs. Fitzwalter one day. "It must</Line>
        <Line>be lonely for you."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I am alone in the world, as far as I</Line>
        <Line>know. I was an orphan when I went to</Line>
        <Line>Hampton. I was born in Texas, and I</Line>
        <Line>lived there with my mother till she died.</Line>
        <Line>My mother was bought by a Louisiana</Line>
        <Line>gentleman, somewhere in Virginia, out</Line>
        <Line>of the Smith family. I've heard her say</Line>
        <Line>she nursed her master through a dan-</Line>
        <Line>gerous illness, and he set her free out of</Line>
        <Line>gratitude. That was how she happened</Line>
        <Line>to move up into Texas when she mar-</Line>
        <Line>ried. My father was free too."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mrs. Fitzwalter spoke of the Smith</Line>
        <Line>family as though the fact of her mother</Line>
        <Line>having once been owned by them con-</Line>
        <Line>ferred a special distinction upon herself.</Line>
        <Line>It was undeniably a widely known fam-</Line>
        <Line>ily. "Smith?" I repeated, pensively.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes," Mrs. Fitzwalter rejoined;</Line>
        <Line>"I've often heard my mother say they</Line>
        <Line>were one of the very first families."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Here Mr. Fitzwalter entered, grin-</Line>
        <Line>ning, arousing the worst feelings of my</Line>
        <Line>nature.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"You have very pleasant rooms," I re-</Line>
        <Line>marked, with forced politeness.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes. I am anxious to procure an</Line>
        <Line>instrument for my wife as soon as pos-</Line>
        <Line>sible. That imparts an air of refinement</Line>
        <Line>to the individual—I should say to the</Line>
        <Line>apartment. I believe I mentioned to</Line>
        <Line>one of you ladies—I believe it was you-</Line>
        <Line>self—that my wife could perform on the</Line>
        <Line>pyano?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I believe you did," with increasing</Line>
        <Line>intolerance. Then, in a lower voice, "I</Line>
        <Line>will try to send you the things on the</Line>
        <Line>list you gave me, Mrs. Fitzwalter, which</Line>
        <Line>you need most, at once."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mrs. Fitzwalter smiled her wan smile;</Line>
        <Line>her lord followed me to the door and out</Line>
        <Line>on the landing. "In reference to your</Line>
        <Line>kindness, miss, I would say that a small</Line>
        <Line>piece of beef would be truly acceptable."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mrs. Fitzwalter had already informed</Line>
        <Line>me that she had no fancy whatever for</Line>
        <Line>meat. I did not discuss the point, how-</Line>
        <Line>ever.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The next day I had occasion to visit</Line>
        <Line>my favorite pensioner, a very old colored</Line>
        <Line>woman—so old that her age had be-</Line>
        <Line>come a mere matter of speculation. She</Line>
        <Line>herself assured me, every time I saw</Line>
        <Line>her, that she was nigh a hundred. She</Line>
        <Line>lived with a married daughter and this</Line>
        <Line>woman's husband, whose prominent</Line>
        <Line>characteristic, as far as I had discov-</Line>
        <Line>ered, was that of being chronically out</Line>
        <Line>of work. He was sitting on the porch,</Line>
        <Line>smoking a reeking pipe when I arrived.</Line>
        <Line>"Nothing to do, Uncle Ben?" I queried.</Line>
        <Line>To which he grunted an inarticulate as-</Line>
        <Line>sent.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"De wages my ole man receive depen'</Line>
        <Line>upon de estimation ob de stone," ex-</Line>
        <Line>plained his wife, coming to the rescue</Line>
        <Line>and to the doorway. I was at a loss</Line>
        <Line>only for a moment, until I recollected</Line>
        <Line>that Uncle Ben had been breaking</Line>
        <Line>stones of late.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How is Mammy Nelly?" I inquired,</Line>
        <Line>making my way into the house.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"She's lively," grunted her son-in-law</Line>
        <Line>again. And so, in truth, I found her,</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>dear old soul! I handed over to her a</Line>
        <Line>small donation of tea and sugar.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"All I kin say is, missy, I hopes de</Line>
        <Line>Lord 'll gib you a front seat in heben,"</Line>
        <Line>she said, heartily. "I hopes I'll be dar</Line>
        <Line>to see, an' dat we'll bofe be a-climbin'</Line>
        <Line>up de mount ob glory togedder. But</Line>
        <Line>I'll start fust. I's a-pushin' on to my</Line>
        <Line>hundreds fast. July, better shet de do'</Line>
        <Line>to. Missy will cotch cold. Dese is</Line>
        <Line>March doin's to-day, sho' enuff. An'</Line>
        <Line>yistiddy was dat close an' sulky."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It allays sets me up fur a week ter</Line>
        <Line>set eyes on you, honey," remarked</Line>
        <Line>Mammy Nelly, gazing at me affection-</Line>
        <Line>ately. "Seems like you put me in min'</Line>
        <Line>ob de Smiffs."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"The Smiths?" I looked duly grati-</Line>
        <Line>fied.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes honey, de fam'ly I come out</Line>
        <Line>ob. Dey is mostly all died out by dis</Line>
        <Line>time, but dey was a fust-rate fam'ly,</Line>
        <Line>fust-rate. Neber seed dere beat. My</Line>
        <Line>ole man he war one ob dere people, too.</Line>
        <Line>Dey was good to deir cullud folks. Dey</Line>
        <Line>kep 'em togedder. On'y one ob my</Line>
        <Line>chil'en was sol' away from me. Dat</Line>
        <Line>war my 'Tilda. She war my eldest.</Line>
        <Line>My ole missus's son he jined de army,</Line>
        <Line>an' my ole missus she sent me ter his</Line>
        <Line>wife ter nuss her baby, when we had</Line>
        <Line>ter go down inter Texas. I kinder</Line>
        <Line>hoped den I would hear somethin' ob</Line>
        <Line>'Tilda. She war allays my favorite</Line>
        <Line>chile. I knowed she war sol' in Louis-</Line>
        <Line>iana, dat's what my ole missus keep</Line>
        <Line>a-tellin' on me. But 'Tilda neber turn</Line>
        <Line>up. Seem like de people in Texas dey</Line>
        <Line>know no more 'bout de people in Louis-</Line>
        <Line>iana dan we do up yar in Varginny.</Line>
        <Line>Hadn't none ob 'em eber heerd ob no</Line>
        <Line>'Tilda Smiff."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How long were you down there,</Line>
        <Line>Mammy Nelly?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I war down dar four years altoged-</Line>
        <Line>der. Two years de fust time, an' two</Line>
        <Line>years de las'. I come up home wid my</Line>
        <Line>young missus, and I went back again</Line>
        <Line>'long ob her. My! it war a long jour-</Line>
        <Line>ney. Dis are a big world. You wudn't</Line>
        <Line>neber tink it, a-settin' yar at home."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"You didn't neber happen to know</Line>
        <Line>none ob de Smiffs?" Mammy Nelly in-</Line>
        <Line>quired presently, after a pause in the</Line>
        <Line>conversation, during which I wondered</Line>
        <Line>whether 'Tilda were yet in the land of</Line>
        <Line>the living.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes, I have known people of that</Line>
        <Line>name, but I am not sure that they are</Line>
        <Line>the same family you mean."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I could see that I lost caste by this</Line>
        <Line>admission. Evidently all social dis-</Line>
        <Line>tinctions paled before the pretensions</Line>
        <Line>of the old woman's former owners.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Smith? Smith? Who had been talk-</Line>
        <Line>ing Smith to me only a short time be-</Line>
        <Line>fore? But my memory failed me. The</Line>
        <Line>name of Fitzwalter did not occur to me.</Line>
        <Line>Perhaps it was unreasonable in me to</Line>
        <Line>expect to remember where last I had</Line>
        <Line>heard that not uncommon name.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"When my ole man die, I tell my two</Line>
        <Line>boys dey mus' look out for me in my ole</Line>
        <Line>days, an' dey do try. But seems like</Line>
        <Line>dey is allays pushed. You has neber</Line>
        <Line>seed my boys, miss, has yer?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I never had.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"De lawyer one, dat's Sam, an' de</Line>
        <Line>doctor one, dat's Isay. Wa'al, ef dat</Line>
        <Line>doan' beat all! Yar comes Isay now.</Line>
        <Line>De doctor one, miss." She presented</Line>
        <Line>him with much pride.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The doctor one dropped into a chair</Line>
        <Line>in a corner, with an air of fatigue.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It's de misery in my head, miss," he</Line>
        <Line>explained; "I has it all de time."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"His head war trepanned," mammy</Line>
        <Line>explained. "He studded so hard, de</Line>
        <Line>doctors said it mus' be done. He com-</Line>
        <Line>plain ob de headache eber sence."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It interferes considerably with the</Line>
        <Line>practice of my profession," Isay pur-</Line>
        <Line>sued. "I graduated at Harvard Uni-</Line>
        <Line>versity in May, but for the last six</Line>
        <Line>months I have had to lie by, and I have</Line>
        <Line>only practiced among the indigent</Line>
        <Line>poor."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Not lucrative patients?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"No, miss."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"De lawyer one he are hired out ter</Line>
        <Line>keep de accounts ob some milkman on</Line>
        <Line>de edge ob de town. But seems like he</Line>
        <Line>earn precious little; not enuff ter keep</Line>
        <Line>his own body an' soul togedder."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Times are hard," commented Isay.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Allays has been, an' allays will be,"</Line>
        <Line>said July.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It are a comfort ter hab a doctor in</Line>
        <Line>de family," Mammy Nelly pursued, in-</Line>
        <Line>variably disposed to look on the bright</Line>
        <Line>side of things--"a rale comfort. I has</Line>
        <Line>had sich a pain yar" (and as she spoke</Line>
        <Line>the old woman put her hand on her</Line>
        <Line>stomach). "Isay he say he thinks my</Line>
        <Line>longs is affected. He hav recommended</Line>
        <Line>some tea ter me dat has help me right</Line>
        <Line>smart. Dat suttinly is a comfort."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Isay seemed noways disturbed by</Line>
        <Line>the confusion of anatomical terms im-</Line>
        <Line>plied in this statement; on the contrary,</Line>
        <Line>his expression was one of gratification</Line>
        <Line>at the tribute to his medical skill. His</Line>
        <Line>sister and his mother surveyed him with</Line>
        <Line>fond admiration.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes," Mammy Nelly repeated, as I</Line>
        <Line>rose to go; "I has all my chill'en roun'</Line>
        <Line>me in my ole age—all but 'Tilda. Now</Line>
        <Line>ef I cud on'y hear sumfin ob 'Tilda, I</Line>
        <Line>wud be dat easy in my min' !"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>A day or so later I was issuing forth</Line>
        <Line>from my own portals, when I met a</Line>
        <Line>young African lady, face to face, of a</Line>
        <Line>certain decorous and dignified demeanor.</Line>
        <Line>She smiled expansively, and remarked:</Line>
        <Line>with an air of enormous politeness,</Line>
        <Line>"Will you be good enough to tell me is</Line>
        <Line>any lady here de name ob Miss Gracie?</Line>
        <Line>I am not acquainted wid de las' ob de</Line>
        <Line>name."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I replied that I was so known to my</Line>
        <Line>intimates. She then proceeded to in-</Line>
        <Line>form me that Mrs. Fitzwalter was wuss</Line>
        <Line>agin, and extremely anxious to see me,</Line>
        <Line>if I could make it convenient to call by.</Line>
        <Line>I promised that I certainly would, and</Line>
        <Line>the gracious person left.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mr. Fitzwalter came by, leading his</Line>
        <Line>little boy by the hand, an exceedingly</Line>
        <Line>decent, shiny, coal-black child of four</Line>
        <Line>or five. Mr. Fitzwalter acknowledged</Line>
        <Line>my acquaintance with effusion. I had</Line>
        <Line>been buying bananas ; I gave the child</Line>
        <Line>one. Uncle Ben, who stood near by,</Line>
        <Line>patted his head, whereupon young Fitz-</Line>
        <Line>walter looked up at him with a pair of</Line>
        <Line>huge gleaming eyes, profoundly deep</Line>
        <Line>and dark.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Land sakes !" ejaculated Uncle Ben;</Line>
        <Line>"dat are a cur'ous ting. How de chile</Line>
        <Line>do favor our Mammy Nelly ! Neber see</Line>
        <Line>de like."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I inspected the alleged likeness. "Very</Line>
        <Line>odd," I said, "but it's so. Well, you</Line>
        <Line>couldn't look-like a better and a dearer</Line>
        <Line>old woman, Sammy. Mr. Fitzwalter, I</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>hear your wife is ailing. I hope to get</Line>
        <Line>to see her to-morrow morning. Re-</Line>
        <Line>member me to her."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I will certainly do my best to exer-</Line>
        <Line>cise your commission, miss," Mr. Fitz-</Line>
        <Line>walter replied, elaborately, passing on.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>My marketing had up to this point</Line>
        <Line>been done in front of the shop, where</Line>
        <Line>most of the wares were displayed. I</Line>
        <Line>now retired within, and made the rest</Line>
        <Line>of my purchases in seclusion. The next</Line>
        <Line>day I looked up Mrs. Fitzwalter, who</Line>
        <Line>was too ailing to come to my house, but</Line>
        <Line>who wished to consult me as to the</Line>
        <Line>alternative of doing plain sewing or of</Line>
        <Line>giving music lessons, both of which pre-</Line>
        <Line>sented themselves to her mind as means</Line>
        <Line>of adding to her income. She showed</Line>
        <Line>me some of her work, and she played for</Line>
        <Line>me a little on the "pyano." I decided</Line>
        <Line>directly in favor of the sewing, although</Line>
        <Line>with reluctance, because I could see she</Line>
        <Line>had a preference for the other method</Line>
        <Line>of earning a living. Moreover, I had</Line>
        <Line>some work I wanted to have done imme-</Line>
        <Line>diately, and which I promised to send</Line>
        <Line>her. On my way out I picked up an</Line>
        <Line>old-fashioned ambrotype displayed in a</Line>
        <Line>showy gilt frame on the table, on which</Line>
        <Line>also reposed Milton's "Paradise Lost"</Line>
        <Line>and Longfellow's poems. The picture</Line>
        <Line>represented a staid, sad-eyed colored</Line>
        <Line>woman (the typical Southern mammy),</Line>
        <Line>a turban about her head, gold ear-rings,</Line>
        <Line>a gold ring on one of her hands, clasped</Line>
        <Line>together in the composed fashion of her</Line>
        <Line>race.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How much your little boy looks like</Line>
        <Line>this picture !" I cried. "Is it your</Line>
        <Line>mother?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes, miss," wiping it with her apron</Line>
        <Line>of any chance dust—"my mother. She</Line>
        <Line>was a good woman if ever there was</Line>
        <Line>one."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Another resemblance flashed through</Line>
        <Line>my mind. I felt myself on the brink of</Line>
        <Line>a discovery. "What was your mother's</Line>
        <Line>name?" I inquired.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Matilda Smith. She always kept</Line>
        <Line>the name of the Virginia family she</Line>
        <Line>came out of. She belonged to the</Line>
        <Line>Louisiana Leveres afterward, but she</Line>
        <Line>never took their name. Yes, Smith was</Line>
        <Line>her maiden name. My father's name</Line>
        <Line>was Willis; so she died Matilda Willis.</Line>
        <Line>She has been dead a good ten years</Line>
        <Line>now. She followed my father within</Line>
        <Line>four months of his death."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I sat down again. "I think—I am</Line>
        <Line>not quite sure—but I have an idea that</Line>
        <Line>I know some of your mother's relations,</Line>
        <Line>Mrs. Fitzwalter. How would you feel</Line>
        <Line>about 'claiming kin?' They are very</Line>
        <Line>poor, plain people."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I should be very glad to have rela-</Line>
        <Line>tions near me. I often feel lonely.</Line>
        <Line>Mother was sold away when she was</Line>
        <Line>only five or six years old, so that she</Line>
        <Line>had no distinct recollection of her</Line>
        <Line>people; but when she was near her end,</Line>
        <Line>she used to say she wished she had</Line>
        <Line>written to her mother, and tried to find</Line>
        <Line>out something about her; that is, had</Line>
        <Line>had a letter written. She never learned</Line>
        <Line>to write herself. I suppose that hin-</Line>
        <Line>dered the letters getting off."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"You lived in Texas?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes; near San Antonio. We lived</Line>
        <Line>there seventeen years—all my life up to</Line>
        <Line>that time; ten years ago, as I said. My</Line>
        <Line>mother was a right young woman when</Line>
        <Line>she died, not more than thirty-four.</Line>
        <Line>That was her age as near as she could</Line>
        <Line>calculate."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"If I find out anything more about</Line>
        <Line>your family, I will let you know," I</Line>
        <Line>said, making another move. As I went</Line>
        <Line>away, I thought to myself, "I believe I</Line>
        <Line>have found dear old Nelly's lost 'Tilda;"</Line>
        <Line>and I felt a throb of satisfaction, even if</Line>
        <Line>mother and daughter could never in</Line>
        <Line>this life meet face to face.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I stated my errand gradually to Mam-</Line>
        <Line>my Nelly when I went to see her the</Line>
        <Line>next day. I reminded her of our con-</Line>
        <Line>versation about her daughter. "I</Line>
        <Line>think I have found out something about</Line>
        <Line>her."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Are she a-libin'?" asked the old wo-</Line>
        <Line>man, eagerly.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I think not, unless I am all wrong,"</Line>
        <Line>I answered, gently.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I cud hardly hab expected it," she</Line>
        <Line>said, shaking her head sadly. "Forty</Line>
        <Line>years sence she war sol' away. Heaps</Line>
        <Line>ob changes comes in forty years. But</Line>
        <Line>you go on, honey. Tell me wat you</Line>
        <Line>hab heerd."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"I have seen the daughter of a wo-</Line>
        <Line>man whose name was Matilda Smith,</Line>
        <Line>and who was sold out of the Smith fam-</Line>
        <Line>ily in Virginia into the Levere family in</Line>
        <Line>Louisiana."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Dat mus' be my 'Tilda. Good</Line>
        <Line>Lor'!"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"So it seems to me. This Matilda</Line>
        <Line>Smith was set free by her master, and</Line>
        <Line>afterward married a man who was also</Line>
        <Line>free, with whom she went to live in</Line>
        <Line>Texas, near San Antonio."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It war near San Antonio dat I libed</Line>
        <Line>four year, off an' on."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How strange that is! You were so</Line>
        <Line>near that you might almost have</Line>
        <Line>touched each other, and never knew it."</Line>
        <Line>I could have wept to think of it—the</Line>
        <Line>joy of meeting so close to them, and yet</Line>
        <Line>they had not met! Where had their</Line>
        <Line>guardian angels been all those months?</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Afterward Matilda Smith died," I</Line>
        <Line>went on. "She left one daughter, who</Line>
        <Line>is living with her husband and child in</Line>
        <Line>Port Royal now. She is Mrs. Fitzwal-</Line>
        <Line>ter; her husband is a preacher. She</Line>
        <Line>has her mother's picture, which looks</Line>
        <Line>extremely like you, Mammy Nelly.</Line>
        <Line>Would you like to see it?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Indeed I wud, chile," the old wo-</Line>
        <Line>man answered, with trembling eager-</Line>
        <Line>ness.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I brought about an interview. The</Line>
        <Line>relationship between Mrs. Fitzwalter</Line>
        <Line>and Mammy Nelly was established be-</Line>
        <Line>yond any reasonable doubt, and the</Line>
        <Line>most cordial family relations were</Line>
        <Line>established. Mammy's whole heart</Line>
        <Line>went out to her little great-grandson.</Line>
        <Line>"My 'Tilda war on'y a trifle older when</Line>
        <Line>she went away."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>I had occasion to interview Mr. Fitz-</Line>
        <Line>walter on parochial matters about this</Line>
        <Line>time. He alluded to the discovery of</Line>
        <Line>his wife's kindred.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It is a series of circumstances, so to</Line>
        <Line>speak," he remarked. "I could have</Line>
        <Line>wished my good mother-in-law had lived</Line>
        <Line>to see this day. Instead of which, she</Line>
        <Line>has departed to the blush unseen."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Shades of the poet Gray! —<Emphasis type="italic">Harper's</Emphasis></Line>
        <Line>
          <Emphasis type="italic">Weekly.</Emphasis>
        </Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>AFFAIRS IN IRELAND.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Heading type="sub">
        <Line>The Arrest of Parnell—Details of the</Line>
        <Line>Affair.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line><Initial type="simple">C</Initial>harles Stewart Parnell was arrested</Line>
        <Line>at Morrison’s Hotel, in Dublin, early</Line>
        <Line>Thursday morning on two warrants</Line>
        <Line>signed by Mr. Forster, Chief Secretary</Line>
        <Line>for Ireland. One warrant charges him with</Line>
        <Line>inciting the intimidation of tenants</Line>
        <Line>from paying rent justly due, and the</Line>
        <Line>other with intimidating tenants from</Line>
        <Line>taking the benefit of the Land act, by</Line>
        <Line>applying to the Land Commission to fix</Line>
        <Line>a fair rent. Mr. Parnell was taken to</Line>
        <Line>Kilmainham jail. His arrest has created</Line>
        <Line>great excitement.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>His arrest was determined on at a pro-</Line>
        <Line>longed session of the Cabinet Council,</Line>
        <Line>at which all the members of the Council</Line>
        <Line>except Lord Selborne were present.</Line>
        <Line>Since Mr. Gladstone’s speeches at Leeds</Line>
        <Line>some of the Ministerial journals in Lon-</Line>
        <Line>don have been saying vaguely that im-</Line>
        <Line>mediate executive interference was nec-</Line>
        <Line>essary to make the Land act anything</Line>
        <Line>but a dead letter. The arrest of Par-</Line>
        <Line>nell, however, was entirely unexpected.</Line>
        <Line>Immediately after the close of the Cabi-</Line>
        <Line>net Council Secretary Forster left Lon-</Line>
        <Line>don for Dublin, and upon his arrival</Line>
        <Line>there by the morning mail at 8 o’clock</Line>
        <Line>Thursday, issued forthwith his warrants</Line>
        <Line>to the Dublin Detective Office. Mr Par-</Line>
        <Line>nell was stopping at Morrison’s, and</Line>
        <Line>was to take a morning train from the</Line>
        <Line>Kingsbridge station to attend the con-</Line>
        <Line>vention of the Kildare Land and Labor</Line>
        <Line>League. One squad of detectives, fol-</Line>
        <Line>lowed by a considerable military force,</Line>
        <Line>went into the railway station, where a</Line>
        <Line>crowd had gathered to see Mr. Parnell</Line>
        <Line>off. It was thought likely that he had</Line>
        <Line>already boarded his train. The detec-</Line>
        <Line>tives went over the train without at-</Line>
        <Line>tracting attention, and the crown sup-</Line>
        <Line>posed that the soldiers had been called</Line>
        <Line>out merely to preserve order.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Meanwhile, under command of Detec-</Line>
        <Line>tive Superintendent Mallins, six detec-</Line>
        <Line>tives went to Morrison's hotel, which</Line>
        <Line>had been carefully watched from the</Line>
        <Line>time Mr. Parnell entered it last evening.</Line>
        <Line>All were in citizen's clothes. Superin-</Line>
        <Line>tendent Mallins found that Parnell was</Line>
        <Line>still in bed, and sent up word that he</Line>
        <Line>would like to see him. Mr. Parnell re-</Line>
        <Line>turned a message that he would see the</Line>
        <Line>Superintendent as soon as he was</Line>
        <Line>dressed, and presently word came down</Line>
        <Line>that he was ready. Mallins took Detec-</Line>
        <Line>tive Sheridan up stairs with him. Mr.</Line>
        <Line>Parnell received them pleasantly, and</Line>
        <Line>asked if he was to be arrested. Mallins</Line>
        <Line>handed him one of the warrants. The</Line>
        <Line>ink of Chief Secretary Forster's signa-</Line>
        <Line>ture was not yet dry. Mallins suggested</Line>
        <Line>that Mr. Parnell go with him quietly</Line>
        <Line>and immediately, so that there should</Line>
        <Line>be no chance of a disturbance.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"All right," said Parnell, and put on</Line>
        <Line>his hat. The two policemen escorted</Line>
        <Line>him to the door, where a cab was wait-</Line>
        <Line>ing for him. It was then half past nine.</Line>
        <Line>The cab was driven directly to Kilmain-</Line>
        <Line>ham prison, the other detectives follow-</Line>
        <Line>ing in another carriage. Mr. Parnell</Line>
        <Line>was warmly welcomed by the suspects in</Line>
        <Line>the prison. Nobody at the hotel and</Line>
        <Line>none of the bystanders on the street</Line>
        <Line>knew that Mr. Parnell was under arrest,</Line>
        <Line>and there was no demonstration of any</Line>
        <Line>kind. There was a good deal of excite-</Line>
        <Line>ment, however, over the news when it</Line>
        <Line>became known, and the newspaper</Line>
        <Line>offices were besieged. On the chance of</Line>
        <Line>a disturbance, the entire garrison of the</Line>
        <Line>city is in barracks, held ready to march</Line>
        <Line>at any moment. It was reported that</Line>
        <Line>the arrest of Parnell was only a prelimi-</Line>
        <Line>nary to still more vigorous action</Line>
        <Line>against the Land League. The Secre-</Line>
        <Line>tary of the League was interviewed</Line>
        <Line>shortly after the arrest. He expressed</Line>
        <Line>much astonishment at it, and exclaimed,</Line>
        <Line>"Let them come on; we are ready for</Line>
        <Line>them!" Father Sheehy, Patrick Egan</Line>
        <Line>and V. B. Dillon went to Paris to-day.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>It is believed that Parnell's speech at</Line>
        <Line>Wexford Sunday furnished the Govern-</Line>
        <Line>ment's technical justification for his ar-</Line>
        <Line>rest, which the Moderate Liberals and</Line>
        <Line>the Conservatives approve.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The Land League Executive held a</Line>
        <Line>long session Thursday at Morrison's.</Line>
        <Line>Messrs. John Dillon, Arthur O'Connor</Line>
        <Line>and A. M. Sullivan, members of Parlia-</Line>
        <Line>ment, were present. Mr. Dillon made</Line>
        <Line>a fiery speech, and it was proposed that</Line>
        <Line>the League should issue an address. It</Line>
        <Line>is said that Mr. Dillon, who is M. P. for</Line>
        <Line>Tipperary, will assume the Presidency</Line>
        <Line>of the League.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Mr. Dillon said at the meeting that it</Line>
        <Line>was the most trying and critical moment</Line>
        <Line>in Ireland's history for a century. The</Line>
        <Line>statement that Mr. Parnell had intimi-</Line>
        <Line>dated the people was false. He defied</Line>
        <Line>anybody to point to a single speech of</Line>
        <Line>Mr. Parnell in favor of intimidation.</Line>
        <Line>His arrest was due to private malice. It</Line>
        <Line>was the duty of the nation to deal with</Line>
        <Line>the matter coolly and with judgement,</Line>
        <Line>and to maintain the struggle within the</Line>
        <Line>law.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>An additional guard and two nine-</Line>
        <Line>pounders have been stationed in the</Line>
        <Line>upper Castle yard. The guard at Kil-</Line>
        <Line>mainham jail has been doubled. At a</Line>
        <Line>meeting of the North Dublin Board of</Line>
        <Line>Guardians, Mr. Kenny, the medical</Line>
        <Line>officer and medical attendant upon the</Line>
        <Line>suspects in Kilmainham jail, stated that</Line>
        <Line>he feared Mr. Kettle, the suspect, was</Line>
        <Line>threatened with spinal disease, and that</Line>
        <Line>there could not be the slightest doubt</Line>
        <Line>that Mr. Kettle's symptoms were due to</Line>
        <Line>his confinement. Mr. Kenny added</Line>
        <Line>that he had reported to the Government</Line>
        <Line>on the subject.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>The inhabitants of Lismore closed</Line>
        <Line>their shops on the reception of the news</Line>
        <Line>of Mr. Parnell's arrest.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Heading type="main">
        <Line>Too Awfully Utter.</Line>
      </Heading>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"<Initial type="simple">W</Initial>ell," said a Deadwood man who</Line>
        <Line>had just been introduced to a Brooklyn</Line>
        <Line>girl, and who had been asked by her if</Line>
        <Line>they had many of those lovely fron-</Line>
        <Line>tiersmen out his way—"Well, mum, we</Line>
        <Line>hev right smart of 'em in our neck o'</Line>
        <Line>the woods."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"And do they wear fringed legs and</Line>
        <Line>hunt those dear, sweet buffalo?" asked</Line>
        <Line>the girl.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"The stage drivers wear fringe and</Line>
        <Line>sich, and when a buffaler shines out</Line>
        <Line>some one is pooty apt to hook on."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How supreme! And those gorgeous</Line>
        <Line>Indians in their picturesque wigwams</Line>
        <Line>of wampum, with their blending com-</Line>
        <Line>binations of war paint, do you often see</Line>
        <Line>them?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Oh! once in a while we get a hack</Line>
        <Line>at a buck, but mostly they are on the</Line>
        <Line>reservation," replied the Deadwood</Line>
        <Line>man, staring. "They does come in</Line>
        <Line>occasionally, but we don't track with</Line>
        <Line>them."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"The sweet things! And you have</Line>
        <Line>such sunsets out in your mountain fast-</Line>
        <Line>nesses, and such loves of highwaymen!</Line>
        <Line>Do you ever see those delightful high-</Line>
        <Line>waymen?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Not often, mum. They get in the</Line>
        <Line>brush, and, as for sunsets, we get 'em</Line>
        <Line>pretty regular in fair weather."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Isn't it just too awfully, too!" ex-</Line>
        <Line>claimed the girl, clasping her hands and</Line>
        <Line>rolling her eyes.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes, mum," stammered the Dead-</Line>
        <Line>wood man. "sometimes its pretty dern,</Line>
        <Line>too, leastwise it was the day that Cob-</Line>
        <Line>ler Duffy came into town on the land-</Line>
        <Line>slide."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"An avalanche! Do you mean an</Line>
        <Line>avalanche? Oh! can there be any-</Line>
        <Line>thing more crystally utter than an ava-</Line>
        <Line>lanche?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"It was pooty tooty utther," hazarded</Line>
        <Line>the Deadwood man, dropping into his</Line>
        <Line>companion's style of expression. "The</Line>
        <Line>cobbler had a—a—ahe had a crystally</Line>
        <Line>shaft up the side of the butte and one</Line>
        <Line>day he was—was tooting around up</Line>
        <Line>there, and things slipped out from</Line>
        <Line>under him."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Oh! how radiant! How iridescent!"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes, mum; and he began to radiate</Line>
        <Line>to'ards town at the rate of 1,000 miles</Line>
        <Line>and three furlongs a minute. We seen</Line>
        <Line>him a—a uttering down the side of the</Line>
        <Line>mountains, ripping up trees and rocks,</Line>
        <Line>and tooting along and his iridescent</Line>
        <Line>wife flapped out of her shack and began</Line>
        <Line>to raise a row."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Poor Lily," moaned the girl; "did</Line>
        <Line>she stop the glorious avalanche?"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"No, mum; not quite. Duffy fetched</Line>
        <Line>up against his shack all standing and</Line>
        <Line>began to howl like a blizzard, 'cause he</Line>
        <Line>thought he'd lost his mine. But when</Line>
        <Line>they'd tipped the landslide on one end</Line>
        <Line>there was the mine underneath just as</Line>
        <Line>he left it. So he could work it right</Line>
        <Line>under his winder. That was pooty con-</Line>
        <Line>siderable too, eh?" and the Deadwood</Line>
        <Line>man never winked.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"How sublime! How crystalline!"</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"But I was going to say we never</Line>
        <Line>had a sun set since."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"So star like," murmured the girl.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes, mostly star like. You see the</Line>
        <Line>landslide stands there to this day on</Line>
        <Line>end, and they don't dare turn it over</Line>
        <Line>for fear of filling in the town, so we</Line>
        <Line>don't get any sun after eleven in the</Line>
        <Line>morning."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"A perennial twilight! So fearfully,</Line>
        <Line>terribly, awfully utter."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>"Yes," murmured the Deadwood man.</Line>
        <Line>"It's just about as utter as you can</Line>
        <Line>get 'em."</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>And she sat and gazed upon him,</Line>
        <Line>wrapped in admiration, while he fell</Line>
        <Line>into a reverie and wondered at Brooklyn</Line>
        <Line>hospitality in not providing "sand</Line>
        <Line>boxes" for strangers.</Line>
      </Paragraph>

OLD BAILEY, YESTERDAY.
CHARGE AGAINST A WOOLBROKER.—
William Jarvis, 56, woolbroker, of Cole-
man-street, City, was indicted for ob-
taining by false pretences from Messrs.
Carr, Glynn, Millis, and Co., bankers, of
Lombard-street, the sum of 3,000l. with
intent to defraud.—Mr. Besley said the
allegations against the defendant were
that upon two occasions—in August and
September—this year he obtained from
the prosecutors two advances of 1,500l.
each upon dock warrants for the delivery
of bales of weel, which he represented to
be of the value of 3,500l., whereas, upon
examination by a competent expert, the
goods were found to be deficient in
weight and quality, and of the value of
450l. only. The false pretence alleged
against the defendant was analogous to
that of a person disposing of a 12-carat
gold ring as an 18-carat gold ring.
The defendant was a woolbroker
in the City, and although in late years
he was not in good credit with the pro-
secutors, who traded with him under
the name of Cousins and Co., yet he had
had an account with the bank for over
20 years, and there was no suggestion
that upon any occasions, prior to August
this year, when advances had been made
to the accused, he acted otherwise than
as an honest and respectable trader.—
The jury, after a short deliberation,
found the defendant "Guilty." They
strongly recommended him to mercy on
account of his age and previous good
character.—Mr. Lockwood, in mitiga-
tion of sentence, said the defendant's
present unfortunate position was brought
about purely through a failure in his
business. The defendant was in a very
delicate state of health, and he had
already been in prison some weeks.—
The Recorder postponed sentence until
next sessions.
This concluded the business, and the
court adjourned until the 12th January.

No paroling on the battle-field; no paroling of entire bodies of troops after a battle; and no dismissal of large numbers of prisoners, with a general declaration that they are paroled, is permitted, or of any value. 129. In capitulations for the surrender of strong places or fortified camps the commanding officer, in cases of urgent necessity, may agree that the troops under his command shall not fight again during the war, unless exchanged. 130. The usual pledge given in the parole is not to serve during the existing war, unless exchanged. This pledge refers only to the active service in the field, against the paroling belligerent or his allies actively engaged in the same war. These cases of breaking the parole are patent acts, and can be visited with the punishment of death; but the pledge does not refer to internal service, such as recruiting or drilling the recruits, fortifying places not besieged, quelling civil commotions, figthing against belligerents unconnected with the paroling belligerents, or to civil or diplomatic service for which the paroled officer may be employed. 131. If the government does not approve of the parole, the paroled officer must return into captivity, and should the enemy refuse to receive him, he is free of his parole. 132. A belligerent government may declare, by a general order, whether it will allow paroling, and on what conditions it will allow it. Such order is communicated to the enemy.

    <Script>Han (Hanzi, Kanji, Hanja)</Script>

  <Page>
    <Header>
      <Heading type="running_title">
        <Line>八大傳卷之一</Line>
      </Heading>
    </Header>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>いふものから活る物は必死す斃し馬に何かあらん。されば又けふの<Emphasis type="underline">将</Emphasis>場を落馬と、</Line>
        <Line>喚ばゝ諱よしあらめ。落羽は落る鳥なれば獲多かる祥ならずや彼方へ行れと、</Line>
        <Line>鐙を鳴らし馬の足掻を早むれば、那古天津等はせんすべもなつ草繁き畷、</Line>
        <Line>道初のごとく先を追して、落葉畷の邉なる落葉が岡に來りければ、宵より、</Line>
        <Line>こゝに躱れたる杣木朴平洲崎無垢三木立の<Emphasis type="underline">際</Emphasis>より佶と見て白馬に騎し</Line>
        <Line>たるは紛ふべうもあらざりける。山下柵左衞門定包也。さはとて、伏たる弓に箭<Emphasis type="underline">夾</Emphasis>て</Line>
        <Line>きり〳〵と弯絞り矢比近くなる隨に一二を定めて<Emphasis type="underline">票</Emphasis>と發せば<Emphasis type="underline">魁</Emphasis>違はず一の<Emphasis type="underline">矢</Emphasis>に</Line>
        <Line>光弘は胷を射られて叫びもあへず仰さまに馬より摚と落しかばこれは、</Line>
        <Line>と駭く天津兵内二の矢に吭をぐさと射られておなじまくらに仆れけり。</Line>
        <Line>すは癖者よといふ程に、徒者等は劇<Emphasis type="underline">騷</Emphasis>ぐのみ敵の多少を測かねて撃とらん</Line>
        <Line>ともせざりしかば那古七郎眼を瞪らし、いふがひなき人々かな。今眼前に主を</Line>
      </Paragraph>
    </Body>
  </Page>
  <Page>
    <Body>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>撃して何か<Emphasis type="underline">躊躇</Emphasis>ことあらん。よしや木立は深くとも、数町に足らぬこの岡の樹を伐り、</Line>
        <Line>草を芟竭しても捜出さで已べき歟と、罵あへず、刀を抜て主に離れし馬の</Line>
        <Line>障泥を切りときて、盾としつ、引被ぎて、走登れば、衆皆これに激され、讐をゝ</Line>
        <Line>定かに認めねども、われ撃とらんと、進みけり。朴平無垢三これを見て、近づけ</Line>
        <Line>てはかなはじとて、樹立の蔭より顕れ出さん〳〵と射たりしかば、先にすゝみし、列卒、</Line>
        <Line>十餘人瞬間に射殺さる。しかれども、彼両人は、矢種もこゝに竭しかば、弓を戛り</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>scriver cose che non vagliono un fico. Ciò ch' Ella mi dice per suo proprio conto</Line>
        <Line>in proposito della mia Canzone nello strazio di una giovane, come lo tengo per</Line>
        <Line>giustissimo, e ne la ringrazio sopra tutto il resto, così lo riguardo per una prova</Line>
        <Line>certa di quello che ho detto; perchè il mio povero giudizio, e l'esperienze fat-</Line>
        <Line>te di quella canzone sopra donne e persone non letterate, secondo il mio costume,</Line>
        <Line>e riuscitemi assai più felicemente delle altre, mi aveano persuaso del contra-</Line>
        <Line>rio. Mi avvedo ora di essermi ingannato.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Le sono gratissimo degli amorevoli inviti che V.S. mi fa di recar-</Line>
        <Line>mi in cotesta bella e dotta città. Ma in che cosa consisterebbe la mia infeli-</Line>
        <Line>cità particolare (dico particolare, perchè delle comuni nessuno va esente, e</Line>
        <Line>molto meno io che sono nato per pascermene) s'io fossi libero di me stesso,</Line>
        <Line>e padrone di portarmi dove mi piacesse? Ella non conoscerà Recanati, ma saprà</Line>
        <Line>che la marca è la più ignorante ed incolta provincia dell'Italia. Ora per</Line>
        <Line>confessione anche di tutti i recanatesi, la mia città è la più incolta e morta</Line>
        <Line>di tutta la marca, e fuori di qui non s'ha idea della vita che vi si mena.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Ella sappia dunque ch'io non sono mai uscito nè uscirò da recanati, non cono-</Line>
        <Line>sco nessun uomo celebre, salvo il povero Giordani che venne a visitarmi a po-</Line>
        <Line>sta, e per conseguenza son certo di non poter mai conseguire neppur quella</Line>
        <Line>fama a cui si levano i più piccoli scrittorelli, e che non si ottiene se non</Line>
        <Line>per mezzo di conoscenze, e di una vita menata in mezzo al mondo, e non del</Line>
        <Line>tutto fuori. Essendo pur troppo vero che l'ingegno il più raro e il più su-</Line>
        <Line>blime (quando anche io ne avessi punto) non basta neppure a far conoscere il</Line>
        <Line>proprio nome, senza l'aiuto di circostanze indispensabili. La musica se non è</Line>
        <Line>la mia prima, è certo una mia gran passione, e dev'esserlo di tutte le anime ca-</Line>
        <Line>paci d'entusiasmo. I divertimenti e le distrazioni, se anche non fossero di mio</Line>
        <Line>genio, sono per sentimento di tutti quelli che mi conoscono, il solo rimedio che</Line>
        <Line>resti alla mia salute già distrutta, senza il quale io vo a perire e consumarmi</Line>
        <Line>inevitabilmente fra poco.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
    </Body>
  </Page>
</HistoricalDocument>

Si vede pure perle antichita come Roma è stata madre di tutte le nationi et recetto de tutti gli Dei di quei tempi che hebbe l'imperio delle piu belleparti del mondo· ordunque cauandosi in un deuerticolo della Via Valeria, per trouare de marmi per far calcina, furono scoperte queste due Basi, et rotte per l'uso che habbiamo detto, oue appresso di un muro edificato di sassi quadrati si leggevano le medesime lettere· et come dimostrano ui è uno epitheto dato à quella Dea d'Artempasa, che non è altro che la celeste Venere;         <Line>1.26. Sicchè il mio credito si riduce a s 2.74.</Line>
      </Paragraph>
      <Paragraph>
        <Line>Quanto alla dedica immaginata dallo stampatore, p. dirle una parola</Line>
        <Line>anche di questo, io non troverei difficoltà di accordargliene il diritto, quando 1. la bas=</Line>
        <Line>sezza ricadesse tutta sopra di lui, vale a dire la dedica fosse fatta intieramente a</Line>
        <Line>suo nome, 2. non pregiudicasse alle mie prove, delle quali la prima non può fare</Line>
        <Line>ostacolo, essendo una dedicatoria di un'altra edizione, e quì solamente ristampata come</Line>

        <Line>do per questo lato l'affare si combinasse, io le potrei spedir subito i 10 o più scudi</Line>
        <Line>necessari per la compra delle 50 copie ch'io ne torrei. Nel caso contrario ch'è il più</Line>

        <Line>La prego a scusarmi dell'incomodo recatole, e ringraziandola caldamente</Line>

mit gmeyner urphet gnedigclich wider ussglossen, sampt ernstlicher
warnung, das er sich dess uͤbertrinckens abthuon und sines diensts fruͤssiger
warten solle, oder man werde in verlauben.
Niklaus Im Hoff Notarius
Barbell Uffry von Fryburg uss Uchtlandt
Demnoch und dise gmeyne mertz uͤber und wider ir urphet, die sy von
einem jrer gschworen, freyenlich onerloupt wider harin gangen, ist sy
jnns Toubhuͤslin gleyt, und uff Mittwochen den nündten Mertzens ditz
69 jars, gnedigclich wider ussglossen, hatt den jnnhalt gmeyner urphet
vorby ouch geschworen, das sy sich von statt und landt Basell
hinweg thuon, und dorin onerloupt nit kommen solle, by peen, byß,
halbÿsens und schwemmens, on wyther gnadt betryssung.
Niklaus Im Hoff Notarius
Hans Sprentzell von der Nüwenstatt
so zuͦ Lentzgich wyb und kindt hatt.
Als dann herren schultheiss und rhat der statt Bern, unsren g.
herren einem geschenck zuͦgeschriben, wie das jrer underthanen
einer zuͦ Lentzgich schulden wellen jchriehen, und als derselb über den
berg gangen, haben jn zwen angsalben, er müsse gellt geben, oder lügen
was im begegne, uff das derselb den muntzel von im gwerff, einen im
arm verwundt, und wie derselben gsell, an den landtman gfallen, in zuͦ
roden strocht, und aber gott im wider uffgehoffen, hatt der landtman
den andren böswilligt, ins houpt verwundet, also das der landtman
von jnen beyd komen. Ist uff disen diewyl er ein wund im

entschuldig erfunden, hatt man in uff Mittwochen den 9 Hornungs ditz 69
jars, mit gmeyner urphet, wider ledig glossenn.
Niklaus Im Hoff Notarius
Geus Hodell von Aistorff
Demnoch Jnnckher Hanss Philipps Offenburg, vogt zuͦ Vorckburg, diser

ihm, vorwelcher gseyt, er welle in beicht, er habe yetzt kein gellt.

        <Line>Om oroligheterna uti Italien förmäler en</Line>
        <Line>piemontesisk tidning, att Bologna, Parma,</Line>

      <Paragraph>
        <Line>— Till Kreuzztg skrifves den 21 maj</Line>

      <BlockQuotation>
        <Line>"I dag på e. m. har under kejsarens pre-</Line>
